title: Suite Maths
subtitle: Why big Cucumber suites go red, slow and expensive, and which fixes actually help

intro.question: What happens to a Cucumber suite as it grows, and what really keeps it green and fast?
body: A Cucumber suite starts small and readable. Then it grows to hundreds of scenarios, runs through the browser, and one day nobody trusts a red build any more. Most of that comes down to a little arithmetic most teams never do.

Five small models follow: ((flaky test)) odds, what ((retries)) hide, UI-level versus API-level steps, ((parallel execution)) and how ((Scenario Outline)) tables explode. The numbers are illustrative; the shapes are real.

formulas.label: Chance the whole run is green
Chance a real intermittent bug passes

steps.title: One percent, three hundred times
body: A ((flaky test)) sometimes fails for reasons unrelated to the code: a slow page, a timing race, a shared test account. Say each scenario fails randomly [[flakeRate]] of the time.
With [[scenarios]] scenarios, the chance that a whole run comes back green is **{pGreen}**. Every scenario has to pass at once, so the chances multiply.

visuals.title: Chance of a fully green run

predict.prompt: The suite grows from 10 to 300 scenarios, each still failing randomly 1% of the time. How often is a whole run green?

options.text: About 99% of the time: each scenario is 99% reliable
options.why: That's the odds for one scenario. A run is green only if all 300 pass together, so the 99%s multiply.
Closer, but still too optimistic: 0.99 multiplied by itself 300 times is far smaller.
0.99³⁰⁰ ≈ 0.049. Nineteen runs in twenty fail somewhere, even though nothing is broken.

predict.notice: Only **{pGreen}** of runs are green. At this point a red build tells the team nothing, so they stop looking, and real failures hide among the random ones.

challenge.prompt: Keep 300 scenarios and get the green rate above 90% by making each scenario more reliable.
challenge.success: At {flakeRate} flakiness per scenario, {pGreen} of runs are green.
challenge.hint: Even 0.1% per scenario leaves only about 74% of runs green. You need flakiness close to zero.

steps.takeaway: Flakiness multiplies across a suite: small per-scenario odds become a mostly red build.

steps.title: What retries hide
body: The quick fix is to rerun failed scenarios automatically. With [[retries]] retry, a scenario only counts as failed if it fails every attempt, and the suite of [[scenarios]] comes back green **{pGreen}** of the time.
But some intermittent failures are real bugs, such as a race condition that breaks [[realFailRate]] of the time. With retries, it still passes **{realBugPass}** of runs.

predict.prompt: You add one automatic retry for failed scenarios. What happens?

options.text: The suite turns green about 97% of the time, and a real bug that fails half the time now passes 75% of runs.
options.why: Random 1% failures almost never happen twice in a row (0.01%), so the suite goes green. But a real 50% bug also gets two chances: it passes three runs in four.

options.text: The suite turns green, and nothing is lost.
options.why: Retries treat every intermittent failure as noise, including the ones that are real problems.

options.text: Nothing changes: flaky scenarios fail again on retry.
options.why: Truly random failures rarely repeat back to back; that's why retries look so effective.

predict.notice: Green rate **{pGreen}**, but a real intermittent bug passes **{realBugPass}** of runs. Retries are a painkiller: use them while you fix the cause, and report every retried pass.

steps.takeaway: Retries make builds green by hiding intermittent failures, real bugs included; fix flakiness at its source.

steps.title: Through the browser or underneath it
body: Gherkin says what the system should do, not how to drive it. The same scenario can run through the browser or call the application's API directly. Here [[uiShare]] of scenarios go through the UI at about [[uiSecs]] each; the rest take about [[apiSecs]].
On one worker the suite takes **{serialMins}**.

predict.prompt: You keep the Gherkin exactly the same but rewire half of the UI scenarios to run against the API instead (80% UI → 40% UI). What happens to the run time?

options.text: It barely changes: it's the same scenarios.
options.why: The scenarios read the same, but almost all the time is spent driving the browser, and half of that is now gone.
UI time is nearly all of it: 300 × 0.8 × 20 s ≈ 80 min becomes 300 × 0.4 × 20 s ≈ 40 min, plus a minute or so of API calls.

options.text: It drops forty-fold, like the per-scenario speed-up.
options.why: Only the rewired scenarios get forty times faster; the other 40% still run through the browser.

predict.notice: **{serialMins}** instead of about 80. Because the Gherkin describes behaviour rather than clicks, you can change how it is automated without rewriting a single scenario.

steps.takeaway: Declarative scenarios let you automate below the UI where possible, which is where most of the speed comes from.

steps.title: Parallel only works when scenarios are independent
body: Cucumber-JVM can run scenarios in parallel. With [[workers]] workers, an independent suite takes **{parallelMins}**.
But if scenarios share state (one test account, one database row, an expected run order), they collide when run at once. To stay green they have to run one at a time.

controls.label: Each scenario sets up its own data

predict.prompt: The scenarios all log in as the same test user and depend on each other's leftover data. You turn on 8 parallel workers. How long does a green run take?

options.text: About an eighth of the time: 8 workers
options.why: Parallel workers only help if scenarios can run at the same time without stepping on each other. These can't.

options.text: The same as before: they still have to run one at a time to pass
options.why: Shared state forces serial execution, or the scenarios randomly break each other, which is just more flakiness.
There is some overhead, but the real problem is that the speed-up never happens at all.

predict.notice: Still **{parallelMins}**. Independence first: each scenario creates its own data in a fresh scenario context. Then parallelism pays.

challenge.hint: Make the scenarios independent first, then add workers.

steps.takeaway: Parallel runs pay only when every scenario is independent: no shared accounts, data or run order.

steps.title: The exploding Outline
body: A ((Scenario Outline)) runs once per row of its Examples table. Testing every combination of [[params]] parameters with [[valuesEach]] values each means **{exampleRows|int}** rows.
At [[secsPerRow]] per row, that one Outline takes **{outlineMins}**.

predict.prompt: A tester adds a fourth parameter with 4 values to an Outline that tests all combinations. How much longer does it take?

options.text: A bit longer: one more column
options.why: A column multiplies the rows when every combination is listed, rather than adding to them.
Every existing row now needs each of the 4 new values: 4³ = 64 becomes 4⁴ = 256.

options.text: The same: it's still one scenario
options.why: It's one Outline in the file, but Cucumber runs it once per Examples row.

predict.notice: **{exampleRows|int}** rows, **{outlineMins}**. BDD examples should illustrate the rules, a few telling cases each, not enumerate every combination. Exhaustive checks belong in fast unit tests.

steps.takeaway: Outlines multiply: choose a few examples that illustrate each rule instead of every combination.

glossary.definition: A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails without any change to the code or the test.
Automatically rerunning a failed scenario, counting it as passed if a later attempt passes.
Running several scenarios at the same time on separate threads or processes.
A Gherkin scenario template run once per row of its Examples table, with <placeholders> filled from each row.

wrapUp.heading: What you discovered
body: Large Cucumber suites fail in predictable ways. Flakiness multiplies across scenarios until red means nothing; retries turn builds green but hide real intermittent bugs; UI-driven steps make suites slow; shared state blocks parallel runs; and exhaustive Outlines multiply run time.

Most fixes come from writing scenarios well: declarative steps you can automate below the UI, independent scenarios that set up their own data, and a few telling examples per rule. The arithmetic simply shows why the advice matters.

In step 5, try 2 values each for 6 parameters, then 6 values each for 2. Which explodes faster?
